emergency.general: Call 112 for all emergencies — the EU-wide number works throughout Hungary. You can also call 104 for ambulance, 105 for fire, or 107 for police directly. English-speaking operators are usually available on 112. Outside Budapest, English proficiency among dispatchers may be limited — speak slowly and clearly, and have your address written in Hungarian if possible.

healthcare.summary: Health & medication guide for Hungary. Emergency numbers (104/107/105/112), pharmacy tips, restricted medications, travel insurance advice, and vaccination recommendations.
healthcare.costForTourists: EU/EEA citizens with an EHIC card receive emergency treatment. Non-EU tourists pay out of pocket; a GP visit costs around €30-50, hospital emergency visits €100-300 depending on treatment.
healthcare.insuranceAdvice: Travel insurance is highly recommended for non-EU visitors. EU citizens should carry EHIC/GHIC but additional insurance covering repatriation and private care is advisable due to variable public hospital quality.
healthcare.vaccinationsRecommended: No special vaccinations are required. Routine vaccinations should be up to date. Tick-borne encephalitis vaccine is recommended for outdoor activities in rural and forested areas from April to October.
healthcare.hospitalNotes: Budapest has several good hospitals and private clinics catering to international patients. Outside the capital, hospital quality varies and English-speaking staff may be limited.

commonOTC: herbal medicines (Hungary has a strong herbal tradition)
medications.prescriptionRules: EU prescriptions are accepted (EU prescription form). Prescriptions from outside the EU require re-issuing by a Hungarian doctor. Some medications that require prescriptions elsewhere may be OTC in Hungary.

restrictedMeds.name: Codeine-containing medications
restrictedMeds.note: Controlled. Requires prescription in Hungary. Small personal-use quantities may be brought with documentation from your doctor.

restrictedMeds.name: Tramadol
restrictedMeds.note: Controlled opioid. Requires Hungarian prescription or doctor's approval. Carry your foreign prescription and medical letter.

restrictedMeds.name: Benzodiazepines
restrictedMeds.note: Controlled. EU regulations apply. Carry doctor's letter and original packaging. Hungarian customs may check quantities.

restrictedMeds.name: Methylphenidate (Ritalin) and ADHD stimulants
restrictedMeds.note: Strictly controlled. Requires documentation. Contact Hungarian health authorities if you need to bring ADHD medications.

restrictedMeds.name: Medical cannabis
restrictedMeds.note: Cannabis is illegal. CBD products with no THC are legal. Do not bring any THC-containing products to Hungary.

medications.bringDocumentation: Carry a doctor's letter in Hungarian or English listing all medications with generic names. Keep medications in original packaging. EU citizens should carry EHIC. Non-EU travelers should carry original prescriptions and multilingual medical certificates.
medications.generalAdvice: Hungary follows EU Schengen medication import rules. Non-EU travelers may bring up to 3 months' supply of prescribed medications for personal use in original packaging with a doctor's prescription. For controlled substances (opioids, stimulants, benzodiazepines), a Schengen certificate signed by your doctor and validated by your national health authority is required. Hungary has strict drug laws — unauthorized possession of controlled substances carries criminal penalties including imprisonment.

connectivity.simOptions: Telekom, Telenor (Yettel), or Vodafone prepaid SIMs at Budapest airport or city shops. EU roaming with any EU SIM.
connectivity.wifiAvailability: Free WiFi at most cafes (Budapest's café culture is strong), hotels, and thermal baths. Good 4G coverage citywide.
connectivity.bestOption: EU SIM with roaming. Otherwise Vodafone prepaid at airport. eSIM via Airalo as quick alternative.

cultural.tipping: 10-15% at restaurants (specify when paying — don't leave on table). Round up for taxis. Tip thermal bath attendants HUF 500-1000.
cultural.dressCode: Smart casual in Budapest. Business dress is formal. Bring swimwear for thermal baths (some require swim caps).
cultural.greetings: Handshake with eye contact. 'Szia' (see-ah) for casual hello. Hungarians put surname first (like Japanese). Close friends may cheek-kiss.
taboos: Clinking beer glasses (relates to 1848 Austrian celebration — some Hungarians still observe this)
Confusing Hungary with other Eastern European countries
Not taking off shoes when entering someone's home
cultural.haggling: Not practiced at shops or restaurants. The Great Market Hall has fixed prices despite being touristy. Watch for tourist-trap restaurants in Váci utca.

safety.lgbtSafetyNote: Homosexuality is legal but government rhetoric has become increasingly hostile to LGBTQ+ rights; public displays of affection may attract negative attention outside Budapest's more progressive districts.
safety.naturalDisasters: Hungary experiences occasional flooding along the Danube and Tisza rivers, particularly in spring. Extreme heat waves are increasingly common in summer months.
safety.pettyCrime: Pickpocketing is common on Budapest public transport (especially metro line M1 and tram 4/6), at major train stations, and around tourist areas like the Castle District. Distraction theft and taxi scams target tourists.
safety.violentCrime: Violent crime is low and rarely affects tourists. Late-night areas around Budapest's party district (District VII) see occasional alcohol-fueled incidents.
safety.soloFemaleSafetyNote: Hungary is generally safe for solo female travelers; exercise normal urban precautions, particularly in Budapest's nightlife areas and when using taxis late at night.
safety.notes: Hungary is a safe destination with crime rates well below the European average. Be cautious of overcharging in taxis (use Bolt or pre-ordered taxis), fake police ID scams, and 'lure bar' scams in Budapest where tourists are taken to venues and presented with inflated bills. Avoid unlicensed currency exchange offices.

practical.visaFreeCountries: US citizens: 90 days visa-free (Schengen). UK, EU, Australia, Canada, Japan also visa-free.
practical.bestTimeToVisit: April-June and September-October (mild, fewer crowds). July-August (hot, festivals). December for Christmas markets and thermal baths.

steps: File a police report immediately — get the report number, you will need it
Contact the US Embassy or nearest consulate: Contact the nearest US Embassy
Bring the police report + any ID you have (driver's license, copy of passport)
Apply for an Emergency Passport (usually issued within 1-2 business days)
Notify your travel insurance and airline of the situation
stolenPassport.notes: Keep a digital copy of your passport in cloud storage (Google Photos, iCloud) and email yourself a scan before travel.

steps: Go to the nearest police station (or call 107)
Bring ID or a copy of your passport if available
Request a written report — ask for an English copy or certified translation if needed
Keep the report number safe — required for insurance claims
For theft: list all stolen items with approximate values
policeReport.notes: In many countries, tourist police stations are available in major cities — they have English-speaking staff. Ask your hotel concierge for the nearest tourist police.

steps: If involved in an accident: do not move vehicles if anyone is injured
Call police (107) and ambulance (104) if there are injuries
Exchange contact, license, and insurance details with other parties
Document the scene with photos before moving vehicles
Contact your rental car company's emergency line
Contact your travel insurance's 24h assistance line
roadsideAssistance.notes: Traffic drives on the RIGHT. An International Driving Permit (IDP) is recommended for most foreign licenses. Rental vehicles are available at major airports and cities.
